title: Doctor Reveals 47-Year-Old Star's Secret: Third Pregnancy Possible with Strict Self-Care
text:
At 47, with three children and a career in entertainment, Han Da-som has defied the biological odds that once labeled her a high-risk candidate for late-term pregnancy. On June 3, 2026, South Korea’s Super Daddy, Where Are You? (*슈퍼맨이 돌아왔다*) aired footage of her consulting an obstetrician who publicly endorsed her ability to carry a third child—despite advanced maternal age raising pathogenesis -linked risks of gestational hypertension, preeclampsia, and fetal chromosomal anomalies. What makes this case extraordinary isn’t just the age, but the epidemiological rarity of such a clinical trajectory in women over 45, where spontaneous conception rates plummet to standard-of-care adjustments are now required to mitigate these risks?
Key Clinical Takeaways:
Advanced maternal age (AMA) pregnancies over 45 carry a 50% higher risk of preeclampsia and a 10x increased likelihood of trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) compared to women under 35, per CDC 2020 guidelines . Han Da-som’s case challenges these probabilities with non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT) and in vitro fertilization (IVF) optimization. South Korea’s fertility clinics are now prioritizing mitochondrial replacement therapy (MRT) and extended embryo culture to screen for aneuploidy, though these remain experimental outside regulated trials. The WHO’s 2023 position statement warns of long-term safety gaps. For women pursuing AMA pregnancies, multidisciplinary preconception care —including cardiology, endocrinology, and genetic counseling—is non-negotiable. Clinics like [Seoul IVF & Reproductive Medicine Center] now offer integrated risk-stratification protocols combining maternal serum biomarkers and fetal DNA analysis. The Biological Ticking Clock: Why 47 Is No Longer a Hard Stop The human ovary’s follicular reserve declines exponentially after 35, with anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) levels dropping by 60% by age 40. Yet Han Da-som’s case—documented in a case report submitted to the Journal of Obstetrics & Gynaecology Research (funded by the Korean Society of Obstetrics and Gynecology)—suggests that ovarian stimulation protocols paired with preimplantation genetic testing for aneuploidy (PGT-A) can circumvent some of these limitations. The study’s lead author, Dr. Min-Jung Kim of Yonsei University Hospital , notes:
“What’s striking here isn’t just the age, but the selective pressure we’ve applied to the embryo pool. By combining time-lapse imaging to assess blastocyst viability with next-generation sequencing (NGS) for chromosomal screening, we’ve reduced the risk of aneuploid implantation to <3%—a 90% improvement over natural conception risks at this age."
—Dr. Min-Jung Kim, PhD, Yonsei University Hospital The catch? These interventions aren’t universally accessible. In South Korea, where IVF coverage is partially subsidized for women under 44, Han Da-som’s third pregnancy required private funding for advanced protocols. Globally, the European Society of Human Reproduction and Embryology (ESHRE) reports that only social egg freezing as a preventive measure for AMA patients—a gap that fertility clinics like [IVI Global] are aggressively filling with cross-border reproductive care .
Risk Stratification: The New Standard of Care for AMA Pregnancies The obstetric community is divided over whether Han Da-som’s case signals a paradigm shift or an outlier. What’s undeniable is the morbidity data: A 2025 meta-analysis in The Lancet Healthy Longevity (funded by the NIH) found that women aged 45–47 delivering via IVF had a 2.8x higher risk of gestational diabetes and a 40% increased likelihood of preterm birth compared to peers aged 35–39. The solution? Proactive surveillance .
Risk Factor Standard Screening (Age AMA-Adjusted Protocol (Age ≥45) Clinic Example Preeclampsia Blood pressure checks at 20wk, 28wk, 36wk Weekly placental growth factor (PlGF) testing + low-dose aspirin (81mg/day) from 12wk [MFM Associates Seoul] Chromosomal Abnormalities Optional NIPT at 10–12wk Mandatory PGT-A + cell-free DNA (cfDNA) sequencing at 8–9wk [Genome Diagnostics Korea] Gestational Diabetes Glucose challenge at 24–28wk Biweekly hemoglobin A1c + continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) from 16wk [Korea Diabetes Center] The table above reflects the consensus guidelines now being adopted by clinics like [Bundang CHA Fertility Center] , where Dr. Lee Seung-hee , a maternal-fetal medicine specialist, emphasizes that “the key isn’t just monitoring—it’s personalized risk algorithms .” Her team uses machine learning to integrate maternal age, BMI, and prior obstetric history into a predictive model with 87% accuracy for identifying high-risk pregnancies.
Ethical and Regulatory Friction Points Han Da-som’s pregnancy has reignited debates over age limits in reproductive medicine. While South Korea’s Ministry of Health and Welfare currently caps IVF subsidies at age 44, private clinics are pushing boundaries. In the U.S., the FDA’s 2024 guidance on mitochondrial donation (a potential avenue for AMA patients) remains restrictive , citing “insufficient long-term data on offspring.” Yet in the UK, the Human Fertilisation and Embryology Authority recently approved MRT for women with mitochondrial diseases , raising questions about whether age-based bans are scientifically justified.
“We’re at a crossroads. Do we treat advanced maternal age as a contraindication , or do we acknowledge that with precision medicine , we can mitigate many of the associated risks? The ethical dilemma isn’t just about the mother—it’s about the intergenerational equity of creating a child who may inherit age-related health burdens.”
—Dr. Sarah Robertson, PhD, University of Adelaide (Lead Author, “Ethical Limits of Fertility Extension” ) The economic incentives are undeniable. The global fertility preservation market is projected to reach $18.7 billion by 2027 (Grand View Research), driven by demand from women delaying childbearing. Yet the WHO warns that unregulated expansion of AMA pregnancies could exacerbate disparities, as only [healthcare compliance attorneys] specializing in reproductive law are in high demand to ensure adherence to local bioethics frameworks .
The Future: Toward a “Fertility Longevity” Era? Han Da-som’s story is less about defying biology and more about redefining its parameters . The next frontier lies in telomere extension therapies and senolytic drugs that could theoretically delay ovarian aging. A 2026 Nature Aging study (funded by the Paul F. Glenn Foundation) found that rapamycin analogs extended reproductive lifespan in mice by clinical trials at Mayo Clinic . If scalable, such interventions could render age 47 a baseline rather than an outlier.
For now, the practical takeaway is clear: Women pursuing AMA pregnancies must engage with specialized care pathways early. The [Fertility Preservation Network] recommends a three-phase approach :
Preconception: Ovarian reserve testing (AMH, FSH) + genetic carrier screening. Conception: IVF with PGT-A + shared decision-making on embryo selection. Pregnancy: Multidisciplinary surveillance with MFM, endocrinology, and neonatology. The conversation around Han Da-som’s pregnancy isn’t just about one woman’s journey—it’s a microcosm of how reproductive medicine is evolving to meet the demands of an aging population. For providers, the message is urgent: The standard of care for AMA pregnancies is no longer static. Clinics that fail to adopt risk-adapted protocols risk malpractice exposure , while those that lead the charge—like [ART Fertility Center] —will define the next era of fertility medicine.
